question: Runner on first, nobody out: a sacrifice bunt moves him to second at the cost of an out. What happens to expected runs?
answer: They fall, by roughly a quarter in run-expectancy tables since Lindsey's in 1963: an out is worth more than a base. Yet the chance of scoring at least one run barely moves, so late in a close game, when one run decides it, the bunt is near break-even.
move: Before judging a move, ask whether the goal is many points or one.
trap: Assuming a runner in scoring position must be worth the out.
reference: Lindsey, An Investigation of Strategies in Baseball, Operations Research, 1963
